props.title: Bollywood/Hollywood
props.initialSlug: Indian man hires escort to please traditional family

sections.content: Bollywood/Hollywood (2002) brilliantly captures the cultural collision between Indian and Western filmmaking traditions through its clever meta-commentary. Director Deepa Mehta crafts a self-aware romantic comedy that pays homage to both Monsoon Wedding (2001) and classic Hollywood rom-coms like Pretty Woman (1990). The film's deliberate use of Bollywood tropes - spontaneous dance numbers, family drama, and arranged marriage politics - while setting the story in Toronto creates a fascinating hybrid that mirrors the immigrant experience.

sections.content: The early 2000s marked a significant shift in South Asian diaspora cinema. While My Beautiful Laundrette (1985) and Bhaji on the Beach (1993) explored serious cultural tensions, films like Bollywood/Hollywood embraced a lighter touch, using humor to examine identity. This new wave included American Desi (2001) and Where's the Party Yaar? (2003), which specifically targeted second-generation immigrant audiences with their blend of cultural commentary and entertainment.

Mehta's film particularly excels in its musical sequences, which serve both as parody and tribute to Bollywood conventions. Unlike Bride and Prejudice (2004), which adapted Jane Austen through a strict Bollywood lens, Bollywood/Hollywood creates its own unique cinematic language that reflects the hybrid experience of Indian-Canadians. sections.content: The film's romantic elements draw interesting parallels with other cross-cultural love stories like ABCD (1999) and Ae Fond Kiss... (2004). However, Bollywood/Hollywood distinguishes itself by incorporating elements of screwball comedy and masquerade, reminiscent of classic Hollywood films like Pillow Talk (1959) while maintaining distinctly South Asian storytelling sensibilities.
